title: BSOD triggered when AlwaysOnTop module is enabled, especially around display sleep/reconfiguration

judgment.rationale: The report supplies three matching win32k double-fault analyses, a repeatable display-transition trigger, and an enabled/disabled control; this supports a guarded user-mode mitigation, not a claimed kernel root cause.
evidence: The reported failure bucket is win32kbase PDEV teardown recursion during repeated display power or topology transitions.
Always On Top was enabled for every failure and disabling only that module stopped recurrence.
The current callback path directly iterates tracked windows and performs border and topmost mutations.
judgment.recommended_action: Approve the deferred-event design while requesting current-build reproduction and event sequencing.

fix_assessment.rationale: No linked implementation covers the callback/display-transition interaction.

proposed_fixes.title: Defer Always On Top window mutations across display transitions
proposed_fixes.root_cause: Unconfirmed: out-of-context WinEvent processing mutates tracked HWNDs, borders, and topmost state while win32k is tearing down or recreating display objects.
plan: Route WinEvent work to the module message thread using immutable event data instead of mutating state in the callback.
Treat display and session transitions as a quiescence boundary; coalesce one refresh after the topology stabilizes.
Validate each HWND before deferred border or topmost work and cancel queued work during cleanup.
Add state-machine coverage and multi-monitor transition stress validation.
verification: On a current build, run repeated sleep/wake, lock/display-timeout, and monitor power-cycle passes with pinned and unpinned windows on one and multiple monitors.
Confirm borders recover, pin/unpin remains functional, and no matching 0x7F crash recurs.

confidence.rationale: The control experiment and current callback implementation support mitigation, but the dump cannot identify one exact user-mode call.

issue_context.summary: Always On Top correlates with repeatable win32k display-object recursion during display power and topology changes.
known_information: The reporter provided three matching 0x7F double-fault analyses and a replacement diagnostic archive.
The trigger requires Always On Top to run but does not require a window to be pinned.
Current HandleWinHookEvent and RefreshBorders mutate tracked window and border state.
inferences: Deferring callback work may avoid unsafe reentrancy, but cannot prove or repair a kernel defect.
The transition boundary and queue ownership must be validated before implementation.
issue_context.analysis: The evidence is sufficient for a constrained mitigation design but not for a direct causal claim. The design avoids synchronously touching HWND state during unstable display state.
initial_investigation: Reviewed the issue, replacement report reference, and fork mirror 622.
Read AlwaysOnTop.cpp callback, refresh, pin/unpin, and cleanup paths.

information_gaps.information: A current-build reproduction with timestamps for display/session events immediately before a crash or safe stress pass
information_gaps.why_needed: It establishes whether the issue still reproduces and identifies the transition boundary that the queue must cover.
information_gaps.how_to_collect: Update to the current stable build, repeat the documented multi-monitor sleep/wake or power-cycle scenario, then add a comment containing /bugreport immediately afterward with the exact trigger sequence.

design.root_cause: Not proven. The defensible hypothesis is reentrant HWND and border work from global WinEvent callbacks during display-object teardown or recreation.
evidence: [Observed] The issue reports matching win32k PDEV recursion failures during display transitions.
[Observed] Disabling Always On Top stopped the recurrence.
[Observed] HandleWinHookEvent calls RefreshBorders and can pin, unpin, assign, or reposition borders.
[Inferred] A message-thread queue and transition quiescence can remove the most suspicious synchronous mutation path.

affected_files.purpose: Owns WinEvent callbacks, tracked-window mutation, refresh, and cleanup.
Declares hook and tracked-window lifetime state.

implementation_steps.current_behavior: The callback path can directly enumerate and mutate tracked windows and borders.
implementation_steps.change: Copy only event data into a module-owned queue and process it on the module message thread.
implementation_steps.code_block: WinHookProc -> enqueue { event, hwnd, idObject, idChild }; module message -> validate hwnd -> HandleWinHookEvent.
edge_cases: Coalesce duplicate location and foreground refreshes.
Reject queued work after shutdown begins.

implementation_steps.current_behavior: Refresh and cleanup operate immediately as events arrive.
implementation_steps.change: Suppress border recreation during a detected transition and schedule one validated refresh after it settles.
implementation_steps.code_block: if (displayTransitionActive) { refreshPending = true; return; } ... EndTransition -> queue RefreshBorders once.
tests: Reentrancy state-machine tests and manual multi-monitor stress coverage.

verify: Build the Always On Top target with tools\build\build.cmd.
Run the current-build transition matrix and compare enabled versus disabled runs.
Verify normal pin, unpin, foreground, and border recovery behavior.
risks: Borders can be briefly stale while a topology transition settles.
Overbroad event suppression could miss normal foreground updates.
alternatives: Disable the module on multi-monitor systems; rejected because it removes core behavior.
Claim a kernel fix; rejected because the evidence cannot establish kernel ownership.

actions.label: Approve Always On Top mitigation design

comment.body: The matching crash analyses and the Always On Top enabled/disabled control support a guarded deferred-event design, but they do not identify the exact callback or confirm current-build behavior. Please update to the current stable build, reproduce the documented multi-monitor sleep/wake or monitor power-cycle sequence, then add a comment containing `/bugreport` immediately afterward and list the exact transition that preceded it.
